_comment: Step 8's requirements, and the only place they live.  `score.py` is the
arithmetic and `evidence.py` is the join; neither knows what this step is
about.  Every path below is a probe's own key, unrenamed, so a gate can be
checked against the report it reads by eye.
This step moves two pins, Rails 7.1 and Ruby 3.2, and this is the only rung
where moving the interpreter is a CHOICE rather than a consequence.  7.1
requires 3.1 at a minimum and the tree arrives on 3.1.7, so the framework
could be taken on its own here.  It is taken with the interpreter because
the application has to end up on 3.2, and 7.1 supports both sides of that
move -- 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 all run it -- so the interpreter can be taken under
a framework that runs on either side of it and a failure is attributable.
`ruby_declared` keeps the weight every earlier step gave it, 1, for step
06's reason; `ruby_runtime` is 1 here rather than the 2 it has carried,
because on an image with one interpreter it is a precondition of every
other gate rather than a measurement beside them (NOTES 13.7 finding 9).
What this rung is really about is that 7.1 REMOVES things, and the ladder's
own instruments are the first casualty.  Every step from 02 onward gates the
adoption of an earlier release's defaults by asking a probe for the list of
settings that are not at their adopted values, and that probe compares a
reading to a wanted value.  It cannot tell "this tree did not adopt it" from
"this release no longer has it".  Three settings this ladder already gates
are gone on 7.1 -- `legacy_connection_handling` and `urlsafe_csrf_tokens`
from the 6.1 set, `use_rfc4122_namespaced_uuids` from the 7.0 set -- and
their readers all answer nil.  A fourth, `cache_format_version`, is worse
than gone: `load_defaults 7.1` moves it from 7.0 to 7.1, so on every tree
that has done this step's work correctly the 7.0 gate reads a plausible
number that is no longer the right one.
Carried forward unchanged, those four would fail on every correct tree from
this step to the last one, and because they are guards from here on, each
failure zeroes the entire gates family -- 0.55 of the reward, on a tree that
did the work.  That is the single largest thing this profile has to get
right, and it is why `defaults_6_1_adopted` is rewritten in place and
`defaults_7_0_adopted` is demoted AND rewritten, both as `absent_keys` over
the readings that survive.  The alternative, editing `wanted` in
bootprobe.rb, was rejected: steps 01 to 07 are calibrated against that hash,
and "the release removed it" is a fact about THIS step, which is where it
belongs.  Step 07 met a smaller version of the same problem with
`defaults_5_2_adopted` and solved it by decomposing one list guard into five
named ones; `absent_keys` reaches the same place in one guard and names the
tolerated keys out loud, which the decomposition could not.  Both shapes are
in this ladder now, deliberately: decomposition when the surviving readings
each deserve a name, a tolerated list when what matters is WHICH ones went.
The requirements themselves are three, and they are deliberately not the
same shape as step 07's.
`load_defaults 7.1` is one line and eighteen readings, which is the largest
defaults set on this ladder.  Nothing in this application BREAKS when it is
declared -- measured twice, 504 examples green and nine pages byte-identical
modulo the CSP nonce -- and that is the honest description of this rung:
7.1's breaking changes are all in surfaces this tree does not have.  So the
declaration is graded by what it turns on rather than by what it repairs.
`config.autoload_lib(ignore: %w[assets tasks])` replaces a line this ladder
wrote itself at step 05.  It is two gates rather than one because the two
halves fail differently and only one of them is visible anywhere else: lib/
reaching `autoload_paths` is the requirement, and lib/assets and lib/tasks
being ignored is the part that a third hand-rolled spelling would silently
skip, in a tree where skipping it costs nothing today.
ERB strict locals is the step's feature work, and it is the requirement that
had to be measured before it could be written.  Fourteen partials are on
disk; ten are rendered and four have no call site anywhere in the
application, which was established by driving the application and listening
to `render_partial.action_view` rather than by grepping for `render`
(build/probe08/out/partials2.json).  The gate names the ten.  It also reads
enforcement rather than declaration -- each partial is rendered with a local
its declaration does not name, and it counts only if Action View raises --
because a magic comment that is misspelt or not on the first line is a
comment, and comments do not raise.  One partial, `landing/_info_block`, is
the trap inside the trap: it is rendered from two call sites with different
local sets and its body is guarded with `defined?(title)`, which under
strict locals is always true, so a declaration of `(title:, html_class:)`
500s the landing page and a declaration of `(title: nil, html_class: nil)`
does not.  Both wrong answers are visible in behaviour; this gate is what
makes the right one visible when the tree gets there by a route behaviour
cannot see.
The two header gates are the exception to a rule this ladder has kept since
step 01: behaviour grades behaviour and gates grade configuration.  They are
here because of a property of the harness rather than of the release.
`cvh/norm.py`'s `_KEEP_HEADERS` is a whitelist and the security-header
family is outside it, so the 386-case baseline cannot see `X-Download-Options`
at all.  7.1 drops it; a candidate who decides that is a regression and puts
it back scores 386 of 386 and is invisible to `defaults_7_1_adopted`, which
does not read headers.  `download_options_dropped` is the only reading in
this task that sees that tree.  `security_headers_kept` is its pair, because
a gate that rewards the absence of one header invites deleting the hash it
came from, and the other five are real.
The demotions.  Seven of step 07's twelve gates become guards: the five
`email_*` encryption readings, `encryption_keys_from_credentials` and
`export_async`.  All seven were step 07's work and are step 08's
inheritance, and a guard is strictly harsher -- it carries no weight and one
failure zeroes the family.  `rails_version` and `ruby_runtime` are not
demoted but replaced, and `load_defaults_7_0` is dropped rather than
demoted, for the reason steps 06 and 07 both recorded: `loaded_config_version`
is one value, a correct tree reads 7.1, and a guard asking for 7.0 would
fail every one of them.
Deliberately not gated:
`strict_locals.strict`, the declaration half of the strict-locals reading.
It is a weaker twin of `refuses_unknown` -- every partial that refuses an
unknown local is strict, and the converse failure, a strict declaration
that somehow does not refuse, is not reachable.  Reported, not gated.
`strict_locals.probed`, the denominator of `strict_locals_enforced`.
`present_keys` already fails when the numerator is empty, so gating it
would be gating that the probe ran.  `headers.html_responses` is NOT in
this list any more: `absent_keys` is true over an empty mapping, so the
same argument does not carry across to `download_options_dropped` and the
denominator is gated on its own (NOTES 13.8 finding 4).
The four dead partials.  A gate requiring them NOT to be annotated would
punish a defensible reading of the instruction and would freeze four files
this task has no opinion about.  NOTES §12 records that they are dead and
why the instruction names ten rather than fourteen.
`autoload_lib.in_load_path`.  It reads true on both trees: Rails puts
`paths["lib"]` on `$LOAD_PATH` through the engine, independently of the
autoload paths, so `add_autoload_paths_to_load_path = false` -- which IS
gated, inside `defaults_7_1_adopted` -- does not move it.  Measured
(build/probe08/out/zw-r2.json, zw-r3.json) before it was left out.
The weights are 0.45 behaviour / 0.55 gates, carried from steps 04 to 07
rather than re-derived.

gates.desc: the application runs on Ruby 3.2 (the tree's own .ruby-version selects it through rbenv).  The framework does not force it: Rails 7.1 requires 3.1 at a minimum and the tree arrives on 3.1.7, so the rung could have been taken without moving the interpreter at all.  It is taken with it because 7.1 runs on 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3, so a failure under the pair is attributable to the interpreter rather than to the release -- and because the interpreter is the half of this rung with a floor under it, which `exists_predicate_gone` and `sass_moved` read.  This image carries 3.2.11 and nothing else, so a tree that leaves .ruby-version behind does not get a bundle and does not boot

the Gemfile's `ruby` directive, `.ruby-version` and the lockfile's RUBY VERSION all declare the same Ruby, and it is 3.2 -- the gate reads the single version the three agree on, which is null when one of them is missing or they disagree.  This is the one gate here whose probe reads the tree rather than the application, so it answers on a tree that cannot boot

and `File.exists?` is gone from the application's own source.  Ruby 3.2 removed the `exists?` aliases on File, Dir and FileTest, and this tree calls one in three places -- config/boot.rb:4, spec/support/save_fixture.rb:22 and :36 -- the first of which runs before bundler has loaded anything, so the tree this step is handed dies with `undefined method 'exists?' for File:Class` at second 0 in all three environments (build/probe08/findings.md §1).  The reading is the scanner's count over the application's own files, 3 on the tree handed in and 0 on the migrated one; it counts CALLS (rules.rb:260-263 asks the AST for a `:call` whose receiver is File, Dir or FileTest), not definitions, and it is a static count and not a boot -- so a tree that reaches a prompt by defining the alias back onto File and leaving the three call sites where they are still reads 3, while a tree that rewrites the three calls has met the requirement whether or not a dead definition is left behind

Rails 7.1 is the framework that boots -- not 7.0, and not a release above it.  The reading is the version of the `rails` the booted application loaded, taken from the running process rather than from the Gemfile, so a lockfile that says one thing and a tree that loads another is visible

and `config.load_defaults 7.1` is the declaration it boots with, read off the application's own `loaded_config_version` rather than off the source line, so a tree that writes the line into a file the framework never evaluates does not pass it

and the eighteen 7.1 settings behind that declaration are actually at their 7.1 values.  The reading is the list of the ones that are not, so a partial adoption names itself; it is 18 of 18 missing on the tree this step is handed and 0 of 18 on the migrated one (measured, build/probe08/out/bootprobe-r2.json and -r3.json).  Each is read where the framework really consults it rather than off `config`, which is why several are read off a class -- `av_sanitizer_vendor` off `ActionView::Helpers::SanitizeHelper.sanitizer_vendor`, `ar_default_column_serializer` off `ActiveRecord::Base` and through `.inspect`, because the adopted value is nil and nil `.to_s` is indistinguishable from an empty string.  Two readings are floats, 7.1 rather than "7.1", because that is the type the framework stores

lib/ is on `config.autoload_paths` -- which is what `config.autoload_lib` does and what the line it replaces, `config.eager_load_paths << Rails.root.join('lib')`, does not.  That line has been in config/application.rb since step 05 and it works by a side effect: eager-load paths are also autoload paths, so pushing onto one gets the other.  7.1 gives the intent a name.  The reading discriminates cleanly -- false on the tree this step is handed and true on the migrated one (build/probe08/out/bp3-r2.json, -r3.json) -- and `in_eager_load_paths`, true on both, is reported beside it as the evidence that the replacement did not cost production its eager load

and lib/ is declared once.  `config.autoload_lib` pushes lib/ onto the eager-load paths as well as the autoload paths, so a tree that adds the 7.1 call and leaves the step-05 line `config.eager_load_paths << Rails.root.join('lib')` standing beside it passes the gate above with lib/ on the eager-load path twice.  The duplicate does not collapse -- measured, build/probe08/out/bp5-r5.json reads 2 entries where bp5-r3.json reads 1 -- because railties pushes a String and the old line pushes a Pathname.  The reading is the number of eager-load entries whose `to_s` is exactly `Rails.root/lib`, which is what makes this step a REPLACEMENT of the old line rather than an addition beside it.  It is a conjunct and not a gate on its own: the count is also 1 on the tree this step is handed, where the old line is the only declaration, and what says the declaration is the 7.1 one is `autoload_lib` above, which that tree fails.  Weight 1 for that reason

and lib/assets and lib/tasks are ignored by the main autoloader, which is the half of `config.autoload_lib(ignore: %w[assets tasks])` that the gate above cannot see: `config.autoload_paths << Rails.root.join('lib')` is a third hand-rolled spelling that satisfies it and leaves both directories as autoload roots.  Neither holds any Ruby in this tree, so nothing breaks today and nothing in behaviour or in `zeitwerk_clean` would notice -- which is exactly why it is read here.  The reader is `Rails.autoloaders.main.ignored_paths`, relative to Rails.root and sorted; weight 1, because the cost of getting it wrong in this tree is latent rather than present

and sass has left the 3.2 line step 05 pinned it to -- which is the property the instruction states in those words, and `3.3.0` is the first release that is off that line rather than a claim about which release stopped calling the predicate.  sass 3.2.19 calls `File.exists?` at load time (sass-3.2.19/lib/sass/version.rb:115), reached from sass-rails while `Bundler.require` runs, so on this interpreter that pin is a boot failure with nothing downstream of it; and the pin was there to hold foundation-rails 5.2.2.0, whose `@mixin exports` tests `index()` against false, which sass 3.3 changed to null -- so the gem and its pin move together (build/probe08/findings.md §2).  The instruction states the requirement as a property of the pin rather than by name -- the Gemfile pins one stylesheet compiler, with the comment that couples it to the other gem written above the line -- and says the pin moves forward to a release of the same gem: this reads that.  The reading is the version the lockfile resolves, not a boot, so it answers on a tree that does not boot at all

`X-Download-Options` is no longer on any HTML response.  7.1 drops it from `config.action_dispatch.default_headers` because the only browser that ever read it is gone, and a tree that has taken the release's defaults stops sending it.  This is gated rather than left to behaviour for a reason that is a property of this harness and not of the release: `cvh/norm.py`'s `_KEEP_HEADERS` is a WHITELIST, and the whole security-header family is outside it, so the 386-case baseline is blind to every header in this gate and the one below.  A candidate who reads the upgrade note, decides a dropped security header is a regression and puts it back by hand produces a tree that is wrong, scores 386 of 386 on behaviour and is invisible to `defaults_7_1_adopted`.  Every HTML response the drive records is checked, and `html_responses_observed` below is the gate that says there were any

and the other five default headers are still on every one of those HTML responses -- the over-correction the gate above invites.  The reading is the five header NAMES (`X-Frame-Options`, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies`, `Referrer-Policy`, `X-XSS-Protection`) and not their values; the one value this ladder has ever asked for is `X-XSS-Protection: 0`, which the previous step's requirement set and which the `defaults_7_0_adopted` guard below reads by name out of `config.action_dispatch.default_headers` (bootprobe.rb:968 and :986 compare it against the string `0`).  The reading is `always` rather than `seen`: `seen` is any response, `always` is every response, and a header served on the landing page and not on the JSON one is the failure worth naming.  Nothing else in this profile or in behaviour reads them

and the two header gates above really took a reading.  `absent_keys` over an empty mapping is true, so a run in which the driver recorded no HTML response at all would pass `download_options_dropped` for free -- `seen` is the union over the responses observed and the union of nothing is empty.  This reads how many HTML responses the driver recorded and requires the eight the drive actually takes -- `/` twice, `/locations/1`, `/voice_answers`, `/numerical_answers` and the three `/pages/*` -- rather than merely one, so a run that lost seven of the eight to 500s cannot satisfy the header gates on the one that survived.  It is what makes the other two measurements of the application rather than measurements of the probe

the ten partials this application actually renders declare their locals with a 7.1 `<%# locals: (...) %>` magic comment AND refuse an undeclared one.  The reading is not the comment: the probe compiles each partial and renders it with one local the declaration does not name, and a partial is on this list only when Action View raises for it.  A declaration that is misspelt, that sits below the first line, or that is in a `.erb` the resolver does not pick is a comment, and comments do not raise.  Four of the fourteen partials on disk are NOT on this list and must not be: `locations/_subscribe_form`, `numerical_answers/_vote`, `numerical_answers/_vote_meter` and `voice_answers/_voice_answers` have no call site anywhere in the application -- driven, not grepped, build/probe08/out/partials2.json -- and a candidate who annotates all fourteen has written four declarations against no caller.  The gate names the ten and is silent about the four, which is the honest shape: the four are dead code this step does not ask anyone to delete

and the suite raises none of rspec's own deprecations from the tree's own files.  rspec-rails 6.1.5 keeps `config.fixture_path=` working on Rails 7.1 by raising `RSpec.deprecate` and assigning the plural setting for you (lib/rspec/rails/configuration.rb:167-188), so the singular spelling this repository has carried since step 01 still works, still passes the suite and is invisible to every `ActiveSupport::Deprecation` reading on this page -- the requirement would otherwise be unmeasurable.  `cvgate/rspecdep.rb` hooks `RSpec.deprecate` itself, and the reading counts only the sites inside the tree, so a deprecation one gem raises about another is not the candidate's.  Measured both ways on one tree: 1 with `config.fixture_path`, 0 with `config.fixture_paths` (build/probe08/out/rspecdep5-r3.jsonl and -r6.jsonl).  One rspec deprecation is excluded by name and reported separately as `inherited_rspec_deprecations`: rspec-expectations warns once per run about the suite's own 22 `.should` call sites, blamed on `spec/controllers/status_controller_spec.rb:29`, and no step of this ladder asks anyone to rewrite them -- counting it would fail the golden and every tree above and below it (/tmp/rspec-gold02.log, "1 deprecation warning total").  A hook that never got in, or got in after the suite helper was loaded, reads null and fails rather than reading zero

guards.desc: the application boots in RAILS_ENV=production -- carried forward from step 02, as a guard rather than a gate because the tree this step is handed already does it
and in the `development` and `test` environments too, each in a process of its own
and with eager loading on, every file under the eager-load paths loading without raising
and every constant the application keeps outside `app/` is still defined once a production process has finished eager loading
the models still descend from `ApplicationRecord`
and none of them has been pointed back past it at `ActiveRecord::Base`
every migration still declares the schema version it was written against

and every one of the 43 migrations the repository shipped still declares 4.2, the release it was written against.  This is step 02's reading restored, and it replaces step 06's `migrations_still_4_2`, which counted misversioned migrations across the whole of `db/migrate/` and from step 07 on counts the one step 07's requirement added: that widening migration declares `ActiveRecord::Migration[7.0]`, because that is the release it was written against, which is the same rule that keeps the other 43 at `[4.2]`.  This step adds no migration of its own, and the inherited guard would still fail on step 07's.  Measured: on the step 07 golden `scan.counts.misversioned_migration` is 1 and the inherited guard fails, which would zero the whole gates family over a file the step asked for (build/probe07/out7/scan.json).  The shipped-restricted histogram is not a weaker reading -- it is the one that actually catches restamping, because a count over the whole directory is satisfied by dropping 43 dummy `[4.2]` classes beside the restamped originals

and the one association this application creates before its parent is known still says so on the association itself -- `Call#location` is written when the call arrives and its location is not known until the caller keys a location code. Step 02 scored this; here it is a guard, because the tree this step is handed already has it and a gate it passes for free would only raise the floor. It is carried forward at all because the gate above reads the application-wide default and nothing else: a tree that switched the default off would fail that gate, but a tree that left it on and marked every association optional would pass it, and this is the reading that notices

and no other association was marked optional to get there -- `optional: true` on every `belongs_to` in the tree leaves the application-wide default switched on, passes both readings above, and gives up exactly the constraint the default was switched on for. The repository has six `belongs_to` and one of them is the create-before-parent case, so the count of optional ones is at most that one
`belongs_to` associations are still required by default

and the five 5.0 framework defaults step 02 adopted are all still at their adopted values -- the reading is the list of the ones that are not, so the evidence names them; the `config.load_defaults 7.1` this step declares sets all five on its way past 5.0, so this asks nothing extra of a tree that has done the work

driving the application raises no deprecation warning from its own code -- the budget step 02 set, now against 7.1's list rather than 7.0's. This is also the only reading of a *production* boot: the collector is installed before `config/environment.rb` is required, so a deprecation the application raises while production boots is counted here rather than by `boot_quiet`, which boots development and test. Warnings raised from inside a third-party gem's own source are out of scope; anything the application itself triggers, including from its own configuration, is in scope

and running the spec suite raises none from a file under spec/ -- taken by a collector prepended to `ActiveSupport::Deprecation` inside the suite's own process, so silencing the warnings does not remove them from it
and booting the named environments raises none from a file under `config/environments/`
the application's own spec suite runs to completion against the tree as handed on, and every example in it passes
and it still makes substantially every expectation it was handed: at least 495 examples
no comment in the source directs a tool to ignore a finding (rubocop:disable, brakeman:ignore, :nocov: and the rest) -- a tree that silenced the checks is not measured by them

every Ruby and ERB file in the tree parses under this step's interpreter -- a file the scanner cannot read is a file none of the source gates can see, so their counts would be lower bounds reported as answers

every file the repository shipped under spec/ is still there (77 of them, listed in pristine.json) -- deleting the application's own tests is not a way to have no findings in them. One fewer than step 04's 78, and inherited: `spec/support/factory_girl.rb` came off the list at step 05's factory_bot rename and stays off. This step drops no further path, so the list it is checked against is step 05's unchanged
every spec file the repository shipped still declares at least one example -- keeping the path and emptying the file is not a way to have no findings in it

the application is still there: every file the repository shipped under app/models, app/controllers, app/helpers, lib and db/migrate is still at its path (98 of them, listed in pristine.json) -- the migration removes what the framework removed, not the application's own code

the shipped spec files still contain at least 220 distinct assertion lines -- the suite handed on to this step has 309, while a suite whose examples have been replaced by a tautology has one; keeping the paths, the declarations and the example count while asserting nothing is not a way to pass the suite

no spec file the repository shipped has been left declaring examples that assert nothing. The count above is a floor over the union of the tree's distinct assertion lines, and a union has a shape it cannot see: one file carrying every surviving assertion and fifty carrying none reaches the same number as fifty files that each kept their own. Every shipped spec file that is still present and still declares an example has at least one assertion line of its own

and every file the suite ships that had content of its own still has some -- the 27 shipped factories, fixtures, helpers and Teaspoon files are judged by existence alone by the three guards above, and `> spec/factories.rb` keeps the path, keeps the file count and removes every object the suite builds on. The reading is the shipped test files that had a non-blank, non-comment line in the baseline and have none now

the tree hands on config/database.yml.example and does not hand on config/database.yml -- the instruction says the configuration is produced from the example, and a tree that ships its own database.yml is scored against a database configuration the recording never used

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) the hand-written new-framework-defaults initializer is gone -- 5.1 introduces `config.load_defaults`, which is the framework's own replacement for that file, and one of the seven assignments the file carries (`ActiveSupport.halt_callback_chains_on_return_false =`) is itself deprecated on 5.1, so keeping it is a deprecation raised from the application's own configuration. The reading is the list of files under `config/initializers` whose NAME is the generated one (`new_framework_defaults*`); the file's contents are followed separately by the gate below, which is the reading a rename has to get past

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) and its contents have not simply moved somewhere else: none of the seven switches that file lists is assigned by hand anywhere in the tree. `config.load_defaults 5.1` is a declaration of the whole set at once, so a tree that declares it and also keeps `...active_record.belongs_to_required_by_default = true` in an initializer under some other name has kept the file rather than adopted the defaults -- and one of the seven assignments is deprecated on 5.1 wherever it is written. The list is that file's seven and no others: `assets.unknown_asset_fallback` is a switch 5.1 introduces and the 5.0 file never listed, so writing it by hand moves nothing out of that file and is not read here -- whether the fallback is actually off is the pair of runtime gates below. The reading is an assignment in the parsed source and not a mention, so the comment in `config/application.rb` that names the switches the declaration covers is not a finding

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) the asset pipeline no longer falls back to the public folder for a name it does not know, AND this application's own audio-URL helper still answers the public path for one, without raising and without warning. Every question this application plays over the phone is reached through `VoiceFeedbackHelper#voice_file_path`, whose argument is a question's short name and has never been a pipeline asset, so the two halves have to be read together: with the fallback on, that call answers and (from 5.1) deprecates; with it off, the same call raises `Sprockets::Rails::Helper::AssetNotFound` unless the caller asks for the public path explicitly. The reading is one boot-time probe of the helper itself against a name that is deliberately not an asset, so a tree that satisfies the setting and leaves the helper raising is named here

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) and so does the other audio path, `TwilioSessionError#voice_file`, whose argument is the error's own message -- the same reading taken of the second call site, because the two are separate code and a tree can fix one and leave the other raising at the moment a call goes wrong

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) the form this application serves is built with `form_with`, the builder 5.1 introduces to unify `form_for` and `form_tag` -- at least one call survives in the tree, so the requirement cannot be met by removing the form

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) and no `form_for` is left anywhere, including in the partial nothing renders -- a `form_for` in a file the next step's author will read as live is the half of this change that the recording cannot see. The reading counts calls in compiled ERB as well as in Ruby, so a builder called from a template is counted the same as one called from a helper

(step 03 gate, demoted to a guard here: `build/gold/03` already passes it, so as a gate it would be a free point -- as a guard it is a floor the whole gates family stands on) and the key is not still lying around in the clear -- anywhere in the tree, under any name. `config/secrets.yml` is the file step 01 created, carrying the same 128-character key in development and test; the reading is every file in the tree that is either named `config/secrets.yml*` (other than the `.enc` and the `.key` that belong there) or mentions `secret_key_base` while also carrying a 64-character run of hex, so moving the old file to `config/secrets.yml.bak` or leaving a copy under `spec/` is named here rather than passed. It is a reading of the tree and not of the framework's own `config/secrets` path, because 5.1 widens that glob to `secrets.yml{,.enc}` and therefore answers `present` for a tree that has only the encrypted file

The loopback header carries a port, so a list written to match the header verbatim fails where one written to match the host does not

and it refuses a Host the deployment has never heard of, with 403. Rails 6.0 puts `ActionDispatch::HostAuthorization` into the default stack, but the list it reads is empty in production and an empty list makes the middleware step aside -- so this is a property of `config/environments/production.rb` rather than of the release, and the only way to read it is to send the header and look at the status

and it refuses the near miss as well: `cityvoice.test.evil.example.com`, the hostname an attacker registers because it contains the deployment's own. A list written as an unanchored Regexp, or as a substring match, serves that host while still refusing the plainly unknown one -- which is why this is a second gate and not the same gate
